subject: Computer Science
titleHi: कंप्यूटर मूल सिद्धांत एवं पीसी सॉफ्टवेयर
summary: Covers the history and generations of computers, classification, input/output hardware, memory and storage units, types of software and utilities, MS Office/LibreOffice usage with keyboard shortcuts, and Internet and e-mail basics. DSSSB asks several direct one-liners from this area every paper (full forms, which generation used what, impact vs non-impact printers, OMR/MICR, time and storage units), so these are quick, high-scoring marks.

sections.heading: Computer: definition, characteristics and block diagram
sections.body:
A **computer** is an electronic device that accepts data (input), processes it under the control of a stored program, stores data and results, and produces output. The basic cycle is **Input → Process → Output**, with **Storage** supporting all three (IPO + storage).

**Characteristics** asked in exams:
- **Speed**: operations measured in micro-, nano- and picoseconds.
- **Accuracy**: errors are almost always human or program errors (GIGO: Garbage In, Garbage Out).
- **Diligence**: works for hours without tiredness or loss of concentration.
- **Versatility**: can do very different tasks (accounts, games, design).
- **Storage / memory**: can store and recall huge amounts of data.
- **No IQ**: it cannot think or decide on its own; it only follows instructions.
- **No feelings**: no emotions, likes or dislikes.

The **CPU** (Central Processing Unit) has the **ALU** (arithmetic and logic operations), the **CU** (Control Unit: fetches, decodes and directs execution) and **registers**. Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine already had this split: the *store* (memory) and the *mill* (processor).

sections.heading: History: from abacus to stored-program computers
sections.body:
- **Abacus**: earliest counting device.
- **Napier's bones** (John Napier) and the **slide rule**: aids for multiplication using logarithms.
- **Pascaline** (Blaise Pascal, 1642): mechanical adding machine.
- **Leibniz's Stepped Reckoner**: could also multiply and divide.
- **Jacquard loom** (Joseph-Marie Jacquard, 1801): used **punched cards** to control weaving patterns, the idea later used for data input.
- **Charles Babbage**: Difference Engine and the **Analytical Engine** (designed with store, mill, input and output). He is called the **Father of the Computer**.
- **Ada Lovelace**: wrote an algorithm for the Analytical Engine, so she is called the **first programmer**.
- **Herman Hollerith**: punched-card **tabulating machine** for the 1890 US census; his company later became part of **IBM**.
- **Howard Aiken's Harvard Mark I** (1944): electromechanical computer.
- **ENIAC** (Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer, by J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly, 1946): first general-purpose all-electronic digital computer; it used about 18,000 vacuum tubes.
- **John von Neumann**: proposed the **stored-program concept** (program and data stored together in memory), first described for **EDVAC** (Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer).
- **EDSAC** (Cambridge, 1949): among the first practical stored-program computers.
- **UNIVAC I** (Universal Automatic Computer): first commercial computer in the USA.

Indian supercomputers: the **PARAM** series was developed by **C-DAC**, Pune.

sections.heading: Generations of computers
sections.body:
Generations are defined by the **switching technology** inside the computer. The year ranges vary slightly between textbooks; the technology for each generation is what is asked.

Key inventions: the **transistor** was invented at Bell Labs in 1947 (Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley); the **integrated circuit** (IC) by Jack Kilby (1958) and independently Robert Noyce; the first commercial **microprocessor** was the Intel 4004 (1971).

rows: IBM PC, Apple Macintosh, modern PCs and laptops
AI, natural language, expert systems (Prolog, LISP)

sections.heading: Classification of computers
sections.body:
**By the type of data handled**
- **Analog**: works on continuously varying physical quantities (voltage, temperature, pressure). Example: speedometer, analog thermometer.
- **Digital**: works on discrete values (binary 0 and 1). Almost all modern computers.
- **Hybrid**: combines both, e.g. ICU patient-monitoring systems that measure analog signals and process them digitally.

**By size and power**
- **Supercomputer**: fastest, used for weather forecasting, nuclear simulation; speed measured in **FLOPS** (floating-point operations per second).
- **Mainframe**: serves hundreds or thousands of users at once (banks, railway reservation).
- **Minicomputer**: mid-range, multi-user (departmental use).
- **Microcomputer**: personal computer built around a microprocessor: desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone.
- **Workstation**: powerful single-user machine for design and graphics.

**By purpose**: general-purpose (PCs) vs special-purpose / **embedded** (washing machine controller, ATM).

sections.heading: Input devices
sections.body:
**Input devices** convert data from the outside world into a form the computer can process.

Recognition devices are favourites in the exam; learn exactly what each one reads.

Converts a printed page or photo into a digital image

sections.heading: Output devices: monitors and printers
sections.body:
**Output devices** present processed results. **Soft copy** is output on screen (temporary); **hard copy** is output on paper (permanent).

**Monitors (VDU)**
- **CRT** (Cathode Ray Tube): electron beam strikes phosphor; bulky.
- **LCD**, **LED** and **plasma** are flat-panel displays. An LCD does not emit its own light (non-emissive) and needs a backlight; LED and plasma panels are emissive.
- **Resolution** = number of pixels (e.g. 1920 × 1080). **Pixel** = picture element, the smallest dot on screen.

**Printers**
- **Impact printers** strike an inked ribbon against the paper, so they can make carbon copies; noisy. Examples: **dot-matrix**, **daisy-wheel**, **line printer**, **drum printer**, **chain printer**.
- **Non-impact printers** form characters without striking: **inkjet**, **laser** (uses toner and a photosensitive drum, page printer), **thermal** (heat-sensitive paper, used in billing machines and ATMs).
- Printer speed units: **cps** (characters per second, dot-matrix), **lpm** (lines per minute, line printers), **ppm** (pages per minute, laser). Print quality: **dpi** (dots per inch).

Other output devices: **plotter** (large drawings, engineering maps), **speakers/headphones**, **projector**. A plotter is an output device even though it draws.

sections.heading: Memory and storage units
sections.body:
- **Bit** (binary digit) = 0 or 1, the smallest unit.
- **Nibble** = 4 bits; **Byte** = 8 bits (stores one ASCII character).
- **Word** = the number of bits the CPU processes at a time (e.g. 32 or 64 bits); it depends on the machine.

In memory sizes, each higher unit is **1024 (2¹⁰)** times the previous one: KB → MB → GB → TB → PB → EB → ZB → YB. Strictly, the IEC names for powers of 2 are KiB, MiB, GiB; disk makers often use powers of 10 (1 GB = 10⁹ bytes), which is why a "500 GB" disk shows less in the OS. In DSSSB questions take 1 KB = 1024 bytes unless told otherwise.

**Time units** (for speed): millisecond 10⁻³ s, microsecond 10⁻⁶ s, nanosecond 10⁻⁹ s, **picosecond 10⁻¹² s**, **femtosecond 10⁻¹⁵ s**, attosecond 10⁻¹⁸ s. CPU clock speed is in hertz: 1 GHz = 10⁹ cycles per second, so one cycle takes 1 ns.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary memory
sections.body:
**Primary memory** is directly accessed by the CPU.
- **RAM** (Random Access Memory): read/write, **volatile** (contents lost on power off). **SRAM** uses flip-flops, is fast, needs no refresh, and is used for **cache**. **DRAM** stores bits as charge on capacitors, must be **refreshed** periodically, is cheaper and denser, and is used for main memory.
- **ROM** (Read Only Memory): **non-volatile**; holds firmware such as the BIOS. Types: **PROM** (programmable once), **EPROM** (erased by **ultraviolet** light), **EEPROM** (erased **electrically**, byte by byte). **Flash memory** is a type of EEPROM erased in blocks (pen drives, SSDs).

**Secondary memory** is non-volatile, larger, cheaper per bit and slower.
- **Hard disk (HDD)**: magnetic platters divided into **tracks** (concentric circles) and **sectors**; the same track on all platters forms a **cylinder**. Access time = **seek time** (move head to track) + **rotational latency** (wait for the sector to come under the head) + transfer time.
- **SSD**: flash-based, no moving parts, faster than HDD.
- **Optical discs**: CD (about 700 MB), DVD (4.7 GB single-layer), Blu-ray (25 GB single-layer); read by a laser.
- **Magnetic tape**: **sequential access**, cheapest per bit, used for **backup** and archives. It is not a direct-access device.

**Access methods**: sequential (tape) vs direct/random (disk, RAM).

**Booting**: on power-on the BIOS (in ROM) runs the **POST** (Power-On Self-Test), then the **bootstrap loader** loads the operating system into RAM. **Cold boot** starts from power-off; **warm boot** is a restart (e.g. Ctrl+Alt+Del).

sections.heading: Software: types, translators and utilities
sections.body:
**Software** is a set of programs. **Hardware** is the physical part; **firmware** is software permanently stored in ROM (e.g. BIOS).

**System software** manages the computer:
- **Operating system** (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android).
- **Language translators**: **assembler** (assembly → machine code), **compiler** (whole high-level program → machine code at once, lists all errors after compiling, e.g. C, C++), **interpreter** (translates and executes line by line, stops at the first error, e.g. Python, Perl, BASIC).
- **Linker** (joins object files and libraries into one executable), **loader** (places the executable in memory to run).
- **Device drivers** (let the OS talk to a particular device).
- **Utility software**: maintenance tools: **antivirus**, **disk defragmenter**, **disk cleanup**, **backup**, **file compression** (ZIP), **disk formatting**, file managers.

**Application software** solves user tasks: word processors, spreadsheets, presentation, DBMS, browsers, media players, payroll, railway reservation.

**Licensing**: **proprietary** (closed source, e.g. MS Windows), **open source** (source code available, can be modified: Linux, Apache, PHP, MySQL, LibreOffice, Firefox), **freeware** (free to use but closed), **shareware** (try before you buy).

**Malware** (malicious software, also called perverse software): **virus** (attaches to files and needs a host program), **worm** (self-replicates over networks without a host), **Trojan horse** (looks useful but is harmful), **spyware**, **adware**, **ransomware** (encrypts data and demands payment), **keylogger**.

**Generations of languages**: 1GL machine language, 2GL assembly, 3GL high-level (C, FORTRAN = FORmula TRANslation, COBOL = COmmon Business-Oriented Language, BASIC = Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code), 4GL (SQL, report generators), 5GL (Prolog, logic/AI).

sections.heading: Office tools: word processor, spreadsheet, presentation
sections.body:
**MS Office** (proprietary) and **LibreOffice** (open source) provide equivalent tools: Word ↔ Writer, Excel ↔ Calc, PowerPoint ↔ Impress, Access ↔ Base.

**File extensions**: .docx, .xlsx, .pptx (Office 2007 onwards, XML-based); .doc, .xls, .ppt (older); .xlsm (macro-enabled workbook); .odt, .ods, .odp (OpenDocument, LibreOffice); .csv (comma-separated values, plain text); .txt; .pdf; .bat (batch file of DOS/Windows commands).

**Word processing**: formatting, header and footer, page break, tables, **mail merge** (one letter merged with a data source to create many personalised letters), track changes, spelling and grammar check.

**Spreadsheet (Excel)**
- A workbook contains worksheets; a cell is addressed by column letter + row number (e.g. C5). Since Excel 2007 a sheet has **1,048,576 rows** and **16,384 columns** (last column **XFD**); Excel 2003 had 65,536 rows and 256 columns.
- Formulas start with **=**. References: **relative** (A1, changes when copied), **absolute** ($A$1, fixed), **mixed** ($A1 or A$1). **F4** cycles through these forms.
- Common functions: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN, **COUNT** (counts cells containing numbers), **COUNTA** (counts non-empty cells), COUNTIF, IF, VLOOKUP, ROUND.
- Error values: **#DIV/0!** (division by zero), **#NAME?** (unknown function/name), **#REF!** (invalid reference), **#VALUE!** (wrong type of argument), **#N/A** (value not available, e.g. failed lookup); **#####** means the column is too narrow.
- Operator precedence: negation (−), %, ^, then * and /, then + and −, then & (join text), then comparisons. So `=-2^2` gives 4 in Excel, but `=0-2^2` gives −4.

**Presentation (PowerPoint)**: slides, layouts, themes, **transitions** (effect between slides) vs **animations** (effect on an object within a slide), slide master, Slide Sorter view.

sections.heading: Internet, WWW and e-mail
sections.body:
The **Internet** is a global network of networks using the **TCP/IP** protocol suite; it grew out of **ARPANET** (1969). The **World Wide Web** (WWW) is a service on the Internet: hypertext documents linked by hyperlinks, proposed by **Tim Berners-Lee** at CERN (1989). A **web browser** (Chrome, Firefox, Edge) displays web pages; a **search engine** (Google, Bing) finds them.

- **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) parts: **protocol** (https), **host/domain name** (www.example.com), **path and file name** (/notes/index.html). Example: `https://www.example.com/notes/index.html`.
- **Domain names**: top-level domains such as .com (commercial), .org, .edu, .gov, .net, .in (India). **DNS** translates domain names to **IP addresses**.
- **ISP** (Internet Service Provider) gives the connection. **Intranet** = private network of an organisation using Internet technology; **extranet** = intranet partly opened to outside partners.
- **HTTP** (port 80) transfers web pages; **HTTPS** (port 443) is HTTP secured with TLS/SSL; **FTP** transfers files.
- **Cookies** are small text files a website stores in the browser to remember the user.

**E-mail**
- Address format: `username@domain`, e.g. `teacher@school.in`. Ray Tomlinson sent the first network e-mail on ARPANET and chose the **@** sign.
- **SMTP** sends mail (port 25); **POP3** (port 110) downloads mail to one device; **IMAP** (port 143) keeps mail on the server and syncs across devices.
- **To** = main recipients; **CC** (carbon copy) = copied, visible to all; **BCC** (blind carbon copy) = copied, hidden from other recipients.
- Other terms: attachment, inbox, drafts, **spam** (unwanted bulk mail), **phishing** (fake mail to steal passwords), signature, forward, reply all.
- The **mailto:** URL scheme opens an e-mail client, e.g. `mailto:info@example.com`.

formulas.name: Storage unit step
formulas.formula: 1 KB = 2¹⁰ B; 1 MB = 2²⁰ B; 1 GB = 2³⁰ B; 1 TB = 2⁴⁰ B

formulas.name: Bits and bytes
formulas.note: Convert bytes to bits by multiplying by 8.

formulas.name: Clock period
formulas.note: 1 GHz → 1 ns per cycle; 2 GHz → 0.5 ns.

formulas.name: Rotation time of a disk
formulas.note: Average rotational latency = half of this.

formulas.name: Disk access time
formulas.formula: Access time = seek time + rotational latency + transfer time
formulas.note: Seek = move head to track; latency = wait for sector.

formulas.name: Disk capacity
formulas.formula: Capacity = surfaces × tracks per surface × sectors per track × bytes per sector

formulas.name: Time units
formulas.formula: ms 10⁻³, µs 10⁻⁶, ns 10⁻⁹, ps 10⁻¹², fs 10⁻¹⁵, as 10⁻¹⁸ s

workedExamples.problem: A file is 3 MB in size. How many bits is that? (take 1 KB = 1024 bytes)
A hard disk rotates at 7200 RPM and has an average seek time of 5 ms. Ignoring transfer time, find the average access time.
workedExamples.solution:
One rotation = 60 / 7200 s = 1/120 s ≈ 8.33 ms.
Average rotational latency = half a rotation ≈ 4.17 ms.
Average access time ≈ 5 + 4.17 = 9.17 ms.

workedExamples.problem: A disk has 4 platters (both surfaces used), 1000 tracks per surface, 500 sectors per track and 512 bytes per sector. Find its capacity.
A CPU runs at 2.5 GHz. How long is one clock cycle, and how many cycles occur in 1 microsecond?
In Excel, A1 = 10, A2 = 0, A3 is empty and A4 contains the text "ten". What do =COUNT(A1:A4), =COUNTA(A1:A4) and =A1/A2 return?
workedExamples.solution:
COUNT counts only numeric cells: A1 and A2 → 2.
COUNTA counts non-empty cells: A1, A2, A4 → 3.
=A1/A2 divides by zero → #DIV/0!.

workedExamples.problem: Formula =B$2*$C1 is in cell D5. It is copied to E7. What is the formula in E7?
workedExamples.solution:
Moving from D5 to E7 shifts 1 column right and 2 rows down.
B$2: column relative (B → C), row fixed (2) → C$2.
$C1: column fixed (C), row relative (1 → 3) → $C3.
Result: =C$2*$C3.

pitfalls: Joystick and light pen are input devices; plotter and printer are output devices. A touch screen is both.
OMR reads marks (bubbles), OCR reads printed characters, MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques. Do not mix them up.
Dot-matrix, daisy-wheel and line printers are impact printers; inkjet, laser and thermal are non-impact.
Transistors = second generation, ICs = third generation, microprocessors = fourth generation. Vacuum tubes = first.
EPROM is erased by ultraviolet light; EEPROM is erased electrically.
Magnetic tape is sequential access, not direct access; it is used mainly for backup.
A virus needs a host file to spread; a worm spreads by itself over a network.
Excel COUNT ignores text and blanks; COUNTA counts every non-empty cell, including text.
Pico = 10⁻¹², femto = 10⁻¹⁵, atto = 10⁻¹⁸; nano = 10⁻⁹. Exam options mix these.
In BCC, other recipients cannot see the BCC addresses; in CC everyone can see them.
Compiler translates the whole program before execution; interpreter translates line by line. C is compiled; Perl and Python are typically interpreted.
quickRevision: Charles Babbage = Father of the Computer; Ada Lovelace = first programmer.
ENIAC = Electronic Numerical Integrator and Computer; EDVAC = Electronic Discrete Variable Automatic Computer.
Generations: vacuum tube → transistor → IC → microprocessor (VLSI) → AI/ULSI.
First-generation computers were programmed in machine language.
Diligence = works for hours without tiredness or errors.
Hollerith's punched-card tabulator (1890 census) → company later part of IBM.
1 nibble = 4 bits, 1 byte = 8 bits, 1 KB = 1024 bytes.
SRAM → cache (flip-flops, no refresh); DRAM → main memory (capacitors, refresh).
Seek time = moving the head to the track; rotational latency = waiting for the sector.
Malicious (perverse) software = malware: virus, worm, Trojan, ransomware, spyware.
PHP, Apache, Linux, MySQL, LibreOffice are open source.
SMTP sends mail; POP3/IMAP receive mail; mailto: URL opens an e-mail message.
